p: The bus station in Adjamé never sleeps. At nine o'clock in the evening, it is full of people, noise and light. Sellers walk between the buses with bread, water, boiled eggs and phone chargers. Drivers shout the names of cities: "Yamoussoukro! Daloa! Korhogo! Bouaké, Bouaké, Bouaké!"

Inspector Mariam Touré stands in the middle of all this, with a small bag on her shoulder and a ticket in her hand. Bus number 7. Seat number 4. Departure: ten p.m. Arrival in Bouaké: around five in the morning.

Mariam is thirty-eight. She works for the police in Abidjan, in the criminal investigation department. Her colleagues say she has "eyes in the back of her head", because she notices everything: a nervous hand, a lie in a smile, a shoe that is too clean.
But tonight, Mariam is not working. Tonight, she is just a daughter.
This afternoon, her sister called from Bouaké. "Maman fell in the kitchen. The doctor says it's not too serious, but she keeps asking for you. Come, Mariam. Please."
So Mariam took a few days off, put three dresses in a bag, and came to the bus station. She hasn't seen her mother for eight months. Work, work, always work. She feels guilty.

Bus number 7 is old but clean. It is green and white, with the words "LA PAIX DU NORD" painted on the side. The driver is a big man with grey hair and a calm face. Everybody calls him Vieux Konan. He has driven this road for twenty-five years.
"Twenty-five years, my daughter," he tells Mariam when she gives him her ticket. "I know every hole between Abidjan and Bouaké. I could drive it with my eyes closed."
"Please keep them open tonight," says Mariam, and he laughs.

His assistant is a thin young man of about twenty, called Lassina. He puts the big bags and suitcases in the luggage hold under the bus. He works fast and doesn't talk much. When he takes Mariam's bag, she sees that his hands are shaking a little. *Tired*, she thinks. *Or nervous.* Then she tells herself to stop. *You are not working tonight, Mariam.*

She gets on the bus and finds seat number 4, next to the window. She has a book in her bag, a detective novel, and a packet of plantain chips. She likes to read about crimes that she doesn't have to solve.
The other passengers arrive one by one. Mariam doesn't want to look at them, but she can't stop herself. It is a habit. Police officers always look at people.

First, a businessman in an expensive grey suit. He is about fifty, with a gold watch and a phone that never stops ringing. He carries a grey metal suitcase, and he doesn't give it to Lassina for the luggage hold. He keeps it with him and puts it under his seat, between his feet.
Then a young couple, maybe twenty-five years old. They sit in front of Mariam. The girl has red eyes, as if she has been crying.
Then an old pastor with white hair, a black jacket and a very big Bible under his arm. He smiles at everybody and says, "God bless you, God bless you."

Then a student with a backpack and big headphones around his neck. A young mother with a sleeping baby on her back, wrapped in a pagne. A very tall man in a black leather jacket, with sunglasses — at night — and a big guitar case.
And finally, four market women who come in like a storm, laughing loudly, carrying bags of food. "Make space, make space! The queens are here!"
Eleven passengers. Plus the driver and his assistant. Thirteen people.
At exactly ten o'clock, Vieux Konan starts the engine. The bus moves slowly out of the station, through the crowd, into the night.
Mariam opens her book. Outside, the lights of Abidjan slide past the window: the bridges, the lagoon, the tall buildings of the Plateau. She feels a little sad and a little happy at the same time.
*I'm coming, Maman*, she thinks.
She has no idea that this will be the longest night of her life.
For the first hour, the bus is a small, noisy village.

The four market women share bread and grilled fish with everybody. The oldest one, a big woman in a yellow and blue pagne, sits next to Mariam. Her name is Tantie Akissi. She sells tomatoes and onions at the big market in Bouaké, and she goes to Abidjan every week to buy at good prices.
"You, my daughter, you are not married," says Tantie Akissi, looking at Mariam's hands.
"No, Tantie."
"Why? You are pretty. You have a good face."
"I have a lot of work."
"Work, work!" Tantie Akissi laughs. "Work doesn't keep you warm at night!" The other market women laugh too, and Mariam smiles. It is impossible to be sad near Tantie Akissi.
Mariam tries to read her book, but the bus is too interesting.

In front of her, the young couple are arguing in low voices. She can hear only a few words. "...the bank..." "...you promised..." "...three months..." The girl wipes her eyes with her hand. The young man looks out of the window with a hard face.
Across the aisle, the businessman is on the phone again. He speaks quietly, but Mariam has good ears.
"Yes... yes, it's with me... No, nobody knows... I said nobody! Tomorrow morning, at the bank in Bouaké, everything will be finished... Don't call me again tonight."
He puts the phone in his pocket and looks around nervously. His eyes meet Mariam's eyes. She looks down at her book quickly.
*What is "it"?* she thinks. *What will be finished?* Then she shakes her head. *Not your problem, Mariam. Read your book.*

The student with the headphones is sitting just behind the businessman. He has his eyes closed, and his head moves a little, as if he is listening to music. But Mariam notices something strange: from time to time, he opens his eyes and looks at the businessman's back. And his phone is in his hand, with the screen on.

The tall man with sunglasses sits alone at the back, with his guitar case on the seat next to him. He doesn't talk. He doesn't eat. He doesn't take off his sunglasses. Once, the young mother's baby starts to cry, and the tall man turns his head very fast, like an animal.
The old pastor reads his Bible. Or he pretends to read it. Mariam sees that he turns the pages very rarely. And he looks at the businessman too. Everybody, it seems, is looking at the businessman.
Near N'Douci, the bus stops at a police checkpoint. A policeman with a torch gets on and looks at the passengers.
"Papers, please."

Everybody shows their identity card. When the policeman arrives at the tall man with sunglasses, he looks at his card for a long time. "Take off your glasses, please." The man takes them off. He has a long scar under his left eye. The policeman looks at the card, looks at the face, and gives the card back. "OK. Good trip."
When the policeman arrives at Mariam, she shows her police card. He stands up straight. "Inspector! Good evening, Inspector. Everything is fine here?"
"Everything is fine," says Mariam. "I'm on holiday."
But when the policeman gets off the bus, Mariam sees that three people are looking at her: the businessman, the old pastor, and Lassina, the driver's assistant. All three of them look worried.
*Interesting*, she thinks.

The bus continues. After Toumodi, the road becomes darker. There are no more villages, only the forest on both sides, black and tall. Vieux Konan turns off the lights inside the bus so that people can sleep.
The market women stop talking. The baby sleeps. The businessman puts his feet on his metal suitcase and closes his eyes. Tantie Akissi starts to snore softly against Mariam's shoulder.
Mariam closes her book. The road makes a soft, regular noise under the wheels. She thinks of her mother's kitchen, the smell of sauce graine, her mother's laugh.
Slowly, very slowly, she falls asleep.
"MY SUITCASE! MY SUITCASE IS GONE!"
The scream fills the whole bus. Mariam opens her eyes. For one second, she doesn't know where she is. Then she sees the time on her phone: 1:07 a.m.
The businessman is standing in the aisle. He is red in the face and his eyes are wild. He is pointing at the floor under his seat. There is nothing there.
"Someone took my suitcase! Stop the bus! STOP THE BUS!"

Vieux Konan brakes. The bus stops on the side of the road with a long, tired sigh. He turns on the lights. Everybody is awake now. The baby starts to cry. The market women are all talking at the same time.
"What's happening?"
"A thief! There is a thief on the bus!"
"Jesus, Mary, Joseph!"
The businessman is shouting. "There are ten million francs in that suitcase! Ten million! Nobody leaves this bus! Nobody! Driver, call the police!"
"There is no network here," says Vieux Konan calmly, looking at his phone. "We are in the middle of the forest. The next village is twenty kilometres away."
Mariam stands up. She takes her police card out of her bag and holds it up.
"Good evening, everybody. My name is Mariam Touré. I am an inspector with the police in Abidjan."
The bus becomes silent. Even the baby stops crying.
"I want everybody to stay in their seat," says Mariam. Her voice is calm but strong. "Nobody leaves the bus. Nobody touches anything. Driver, please lock the door."
Vieux Konan locks the door. The businessman looks at Mariam with surprise, then with relief.
"Thank God! Inspector, you must find my suitcase. You must!"
"Sit down, sir. What is your name?"
"Assi. Bernard Assi. I am a businessman. Construction."
"Mr. Assi, when did you last see your suitcase?"

He sits down heavily. He wipes his face with a handkerchief. "I... I was awake all the time. Well, almost. I closed my eyes for twenty minutes, maybe thirty. Before that, the suitcase was there, under my feet. I'm sure. When I woke up, it was gone."
"Did the bus stop while you were sleeping?"
Mariam looks at Vieux Konan. The old driver shakes his head. "No, Inspector. Not since the checkpoint at Toumodi. Not one time."
"And the door was closed?"
"Always closed. It only opens when I press the button."

Mariam thinks. She looks at the bus: twelve rows of seats, a narrow aisle, the driver's place at the front, a small toilet at the back that doesn't work. The luggage hold is under the bus, and you can only open it from outside.
"So," she says slowly, "the suitcase disappeared in the last thirty minutes. The bus did not stop. The door did not open. Nobody got off."
She looks at the passengers, one by one.
"That means the suitcase is still here. On this bus. And the person who took it is still here too."

Nobody speaks. People look at each other with suspicious eyes. The young couple hold hands. The student takes off his headphones. The tall man in the sunglasses doesn't move at all. The pastor closes his eyes and moves his lips, as if he is praying.
Tantie Akissi crosses her arms. "Inspector, I am a market woman. I have been robbed many times in my life. I can tell you one thing: the thief is always the person who looks the most innocent."
"Thank you, Tantie," says Mariam. "I will remember that."
Outside, in the darkness, the insects are singing. The forest is very big and very black. Somewhere far away, a dog barks.
Mariam looks at her watch. Ten past one. The sun rises at six. She has five hours.
*So much for my holiday*, she thinks. Then she takes a pen and a small notebook out of her bag.
"OK," she says. "Let's begin."
Mariam decides to talk to every passenger, one by one, at the front of the bus, near the driver. The others must stay in their seats. Vieux Konan watches the aisle in his big mirror.
"Like a real police station," he says. "But with better air conditioning."
The first people are the young couple. Their names are Koffi and Ruth. They are getting married in Bouaké in two weeks.
"Why were you arguing?" asks Mariam.

Koffi looks at the floor. Ruth answers. "Money, Inspector. Koffi borrowed money from a bank for the wedding. A lot of money. Now he can't pay it back. The bank says he has three months, or they take his car."
"How much do you owe?"
"Two million francs," says Koffi quietly.

Mariam writes in her notebook. *Koffi and Ruth. Debt: 2 million. Need money. Motive?* She looks at their hands. Ruth's hands are small and clean. Koffi's hands are big, with dirty nails. A mechanic, maybe.
"Did you sleep, between half past twelve and one o'clock?"
"I slept," says Ruth. "I was tired of crying."
"I didn't sleep," says Koffi. "I was thinking about the money."
"Did you see anything?"
Koffi hesitates. "It was dark. I saw... someone walk to the back of the bus. And come back. But I don't know who. It was too dark."
The second person is the student. He is about twenty-two, thin, with glasses and a T-shirt that says *JOURNALISM IS NOT A CRIME*.
"My name is Ibrahim Coulibaly. I'm a student at the university in Abidjan. I'm going home to Bouaké for the holidays."
"You were listening to music with your headphones?"
"Yes. I didn't hear anything. I was listening to music all the time."
Mariam looks at the headphones around his neck. Then she takes the cable in her fingers. The end of the cable is free. It is not connected to his phone. It is not connected to anything.
"Ibrahim," she says softly. "Your headphones are not connected."
The student becomes very red. He opens his mouth and closes it again.
"I think you were not listening to music," says Mariam. "I think you were listening to Mr. Assi. You were listening to his phone calls. Why?"
Ibrahim looks down the bus, at the businessman. Then he says, in a very low voice: "I can't tell you here. Not now. But I didn't take his suitcase, Inspector. I swear on my mother's life."
Mariam looks at him for a long moment. *He is scared*, she thinks. *But he is not lying. Or he is a very good liar.* She writes in her notebook: *Ibrahim. Spying on Assi. Why?*
The third person is the tall man with the sunglasses. He sits down slowly. He is so tall that his knees touch the seat in front of him.
"Your name, please."
"People call me Black Diamond. I'm a musician. I play the guitar in a band. We have a concert in Bouaké on Saturday."
"Your real name?"
A pause. "Yao. Yao Kouamé."
"Why do you wear sunglasses at night, Mr. Kouamé?"
"My eyes are sensitive to light. A medical problem."
"And the scar under your eye?"
He doesn't answer for a moment. Then he says: "An accident. A long time ago."
Mariam doesn't believe him. She knows scars. That is a knife scar.
"Did you leave your seat tonight?"
"No."
"Not once?"
"No."
But Mariam remembers something from Koffi's answer. *Someone walked to the back of the bus.* The tall man's seat is already at the back. If he moved, he moved towards the front. Towards Mr. Assi.
"Can I look in your guitar case?"
Black Diamond's face doesn't change. But his hands close very tightly on his knees.
"Later," says Mariam, before he can answer. "First I want to talk to everybody. Go back to your seat, please."
When he leaves, Mariam looks at her notebook. Three passengers. Three secrets. A couple with debts. A student who spies. A musician who lies.
*And eight more people to go*, she thinks.
She looks at her watch. Twenty-five to two.
The next person is the young mother. Her baby is awake now, and he looks at Mariam with big, serious eyes.
"My name is Fanta. This is my son, Junior. He is seven months old. We are going to see his father in Bouaké. He is a soldier there."
"Did you sleep tonight, Fanta?"

"No, Inspector. Junior cried at half past twelve. He always cries at night. I didn't want him to wake up everybody, so I walked to the back of the bus with him. I stayed there for ten minutes, maybe fifteen, and I sang to him."
Mariam sits up. "You were at the back of the bus between half past twelve and a quarter to one?"
"Yes."
"Did you see anything? Anything strange?"

Fanta thinks. She rocks Junior gently. "It was dark. Most people were sleeping. The musician was sleeping, I think, with his head against the window." She stops. "But the driver's assistant was there. The young one."
"Lassina?"

"Yes. He was at the back, near the emergency door. He was doing something with the bags. One bag fell, I heard it. He said to me, 'Sorry, madame, everything's fine, go and sit down.' He seemed... nervous."
"Did you see a grey metal suitcase?"
Fanta shakes her head. "I don't know. It was very dark. I'm sorry."
Mariam writes: *Fanta. At back 12:30–12:45. Saw Lassina at emergency door. Bag fell.*
The emergency door. Mariam had forgotten it. At the back of every bus, there is an emergency door. It opens from inside. And behind it... the road. And under the bus, the luggage hold.
She calls Lassina.
The young man comes to the front. He is thin and his eyes don't stay still. He doesn't sit down.
"Lassina, what were you doing at the back of the bus at half past twelve?"
"Nothing, Inspector! A bag fell from the shelf above the seats. I put it back. That's all. I swear!"
"Whose bag?"
"I... I don't know. A black bag. I put it back."
"Did you open the emergency door?"
Lassina's face becomes grey. "No! Why would I open it? The bus was moving. It's dangerous!"

Vieux Konan turns around in his seat. He looks at his assistant for a long time. "Lassina," he says quietly. "You have worked with me for two years. You are a good boy. If you have something to say, say it now."
Lassina's lips tremble. For a moment, Mariam thinks he will speak. Then he looks down the bus — towards the old pastor — and he closes his mouth.
"I have nothing to say, Vieux Père."
Mariam notices the look. *Lassina looked at the pastor. Why?*
While she is thinking, Ibrahim the student comes to the front again. He leans close to Mariam and speaks very quietly, so that only she can hear.

"Inspector, I want to tell you my secret now. I'm a student in journalism. For six months, I have been investigating Mr. Assi. He is a very rich man, but I think he is a thief. I think he steals public money."
"What kind of money?"

"Money for schools. For roads. For health centres in villages. The government and the villages give him money to build, and he builds nothing — or he builds very badly. Tonight, I heard him on the phone. He said: 'The school money is with me. Tomorrow at the bank in Bouaké, I change it into dollars, and then it's finished. Nobody will find it.' I recorded it on my phone."
He shows Mariam his phone. She listens to the recording with one earphone. It is Mr. Assi's voice. Very clear.
Mariam looks at Mr. Assi. He is sitting in his seat, wiping his face with his handkerchief, talking angrily to nobody.
"The school money," she repeats slowly.
Suddenly, the case is not so simple. The thief may be a criminal. But the victim may be a criminal too.
It is two o'clock. Mariam stands in the aisle and looks at everybody.
"I'm going to search the bus," she says. "The seats, the shelves, the bags. Everything. If you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear."

The market women open their bags immediately. "Search, my daughter, search! Tomatoes, onions, dried fish, and my husband's medicine. If you find ten million francs in there, please tell me, because I want it!"
Everybody laughs, even Mariam. It feels good.

She searches the market women's bags, the couple's bags, Fanta's bag with the baby's bottles and clothes, Ibrahim's backpack full of books. She looks under every seat. She looks on every shelf. Nothing. No grey metal suitcase.
Then she arrives at the back of the bus, at the tall musician.
"Mr. Kouamé. Your guitar case, please."
Black Diamond doesn't move.
"Mr. Kouamé," says Mariam again, calmly. "Open the case, or I will open it."
The whole bus is watching. Slowly, the tall man puts the guitar case on his knees. He opens the first lock. Then the second. He lifts the top.
Inside, there is a guitar. A beautiful old guitar, brown and gold, with a picture of a woman stuck on it.
That's all. Only a guitar.
Mariam lifts the guitar carefully. Under it, there is nothing. She knocks on the bottom of the case. It is not a false bottom.
"Satisfied, Inspector?" says Black Diamond. His voice is cold.
But Mariam has seen something. When he opened the case, his hand pushed something small and white deeper into his jacket. Paper. An envelope.
"Mr. Kouamé. What is in your jacket?"
For the first time, the musician takes off his sunglasses. His eyes are tired and very sad.
"Please, Inspector. Not in front of everybody."
Mariam looks at him. Then she nods. "Come to the front."

At the front, near Vieux Konan, Black Diamond gives her the envelope. It is a letter from a prison. Bouaké prison. The letter is to a man called Yao Kouamé: *You are free from today. You must report to the police station in Bouaké every month for two years.*

"I was in prison for six years," says Black Diamond quietly. "A fight. A long time ago, when I was young and stupid. A man attacked my little brother with a knife, and I hit him too hard. The scar is from that night."
He looks at his hands.

"I got out last year. Now I play music. I'm trying to have a normal life. But when people learn I was in prison, they look at me like a monster. When the policeman at the checkpoint looked at my card, I was terrified. And when you said you were a police inspector... I thought, *that's it. They will say it was me. They always say it was me.*"
"That's why you lied," says Mariam.
"Yes. I'm sorry. But I did not take that suitcase. I slept from Toumodi to the scream. I swear."
Mariam gives him back his letter. "Put your sunglasses back on if you want. But don't lie to me again."
"Yes, Inspector. Thank you, Inspector."
He goes back to his seat. Mariam looks at her notebook.
*Black Diamond — not him. Probably.*

Who is left? The four market women, who are too busy laughing to steal anything. Fanta, with her baby. The couple. Ibrahim. Lassina, who is lying about something. And the old pastor with his big Bible, who hasn't said one word since the scream.
Mariam walks slowly down the aisle again. She looks at the floor. She looks at the seats. And then she stops next to the pastor, and she looks at his shoes.
They are covered in red dust. Red earth. The kind of earth you find on village roads, not in Abidjan. But the pastor got on the bus in Adjamé, like everybody else.
And under the dust, on the side of the left shoe, there is a small, fresh, black mark. Like engine oil.
Mariam doesn't say anything about the shoes. Not yet. She smiles at the old pastor and walks to the back of the bus.
The emergency door is closed. Next to it, there is the small toilet. On the door, someone has written in black marker: *OUT OF ORDER — DO NOT USE.*
"Driver," Mariam calls. "This toilet. Is it locked?"
"Yes, Inspector," says Vieux Konan. "It has been broken for three months. Oil from the engine comes into it, under the floor. The company never repairs anything. Only Lassina has the key."
Mariam turns around. Lassina is standing in the aisle. His face is the colour of ash.
"Lassina," says Mariam gently. "The key, please."
For a long moment, the young man doesn't move. Then, with a shaking hand, he takes a small key out of his pocket and gives it to her.
Mariam opens the toilet door.
The smell of engine oil comes out. The floor is black and dirty. And there, on the floor, next to the broken toilet, is a grey metal suitcase.
"MY SUITCASE!" shouts Mr. Assi, jumping up. "That's my suitcase! I knew it! The boy is the thief! Arrest him!"
"Sit down, Mr. Assi," says Mariam, without turning around.
She lifts the suitcase. It is very light. She puts it on a seat and opens it. It is not locked.
Inside, there is no money.

There are only papers. Many papers, in plastic folders. Mariam takes one and reads it. It is a contract. *Construction of a primary school with six classrooms in the village of Assékro. Amount: 48,000,000 francs. Contractor: ASSI CONSTRUCTION.* There are photos too: photos of a beautiful new school, white and blue, with children in uniforms in front of it.
And there is a second photo, older, of a field with grass and three wooden posts. On the back of the second photo, someone has written in pencil: *Assékro, last month. The "school".*
Mariam looks at Mr. Assi. He is not red anymore. He is white.
"Where is the money, Inspector?" he says. His voice is not so strong now. "There were ten million francs in that suitcase. Where is it?"
Mariam walks slowly back up the aisle. She stops next to the old pastor.
"Pastor, that's a very big Bible," she says.
The old man looks up at her. His eyes are calm and very tired.
"The word of God is big, my daughter."
"May I see it?"
The pastor doesn't answer. He doesn't move. Then he gives a long sigh, and he puts the big black Bible in Mariam's hands.
It is heavy. Too heavy. Mariam opens it.

The first ten pages are real pages, from Genesis. After that, the pages are cut. Somebody has cut a big square hole in the middle of the book, through hundreds of pages. And the hole is full of money: thick packets of ten-thousand-franc notes, held together with rubber bands. On top of the money, there is a small silver key.
The whole bus is silent. One of the market women says, very quietly, "Jesus, Mary, Joseph."
Mariam takes the small key and holds it up.
"This key opens Mr. Assi's suitcase, doesn't it, Pastor?"
"Yes," says the old man.
"And you took the money out of the suitcase, and Lassina hid the empty suitcase in the toilet, at half past twelve, while Fanta was singing to her baby and everybody else was asleep."
The old man looks at Lassina. Lassina is crying silently.
"Don't blame the boy," says the pastor. "It was my idea. All of it."
"Then who are you?" asks Mariam. "Because I don't think you are a pastor."
The old man takes off his black jacket. He folds it carefully on his knees. Then he looks at Mariam, and for the first time tonight, he doesn't smile.
"My name is Joseph Kouassi," he says. "I am not a pastor. I am a teacher. For thirty-one years, I taught the children of Assékro under a mango tree, because we never had a school."
He looks at Mr. Assi.
"And that man stole our school."
Nobody on the bus is sleeping now. Even little Junior is quiet, as if he wants to hear the story too.
Joseph Kouassi speaks slowly. He has the voice of a teacher: clear, patient, made to be heard at the back of a class.

"Assékro is a small village, thirty kilometres from Bouaké. Six hundred people. Farmers. Cotton, yams, cashew nuts. Good people. Poor people. For thirty-one years, I taught the children under a mango tree. When it rained, we stopped. When the sun was too hot, we stopped. Our children learned to read with books that had no covers and no last pages."
He smiles a little. "Some of my students never knew how the stories ended."

"Three years ago, we had a miracle. The government gave money to build a school in Assékro. Forty-eight million francs. And the people of the village gave money too. Everybody gave something. Farmers sold goats. Women sold their jewellery. Old people gave the money they kept for their own funerals. We collected ten million more, for desks, books and a water pump."
He looks at Mr. Assi.

"The government chose a construction company. Assi Construction. Mr. Bernard Assi came to Assékro in a big car. He shook everybody's hand. He promised a beautiful school in one year. The village chief gave him our ten million too, so he could buy everything together. We were so happy. We danced all night."
His voice becomes quiet.

"That was three years ago. Today, in Assékro, there are three wooden posts in a field. That's all. Three posts. And Mr. Assi sent beautiful photos to the government — photos of a school in another town, with a new name painted on it. The government thinks our school exists. The children still learn under the mango tree."
Mr. Assi stands up. "Lies! All lies! This old man is crazy! He is a thief, you saw it yourself, Inspector! He stole my money!"

"Your money?" says Joseph, very calmly. "Last week, the village chief got a letter. Your company is closing. You are leaving the country. And the money of Assékro — our ten million francs, our goats, our jewellery, our funerals — you took it out of the bank in cash. You were taking it to Bouaké tonight, to change it into dollars. Then you would disappear."
Ibrahim the student holds up his phone. "It's true, Inspector. I have the recording. He said it himself."
Mr. Assi sits down again. He doesn't say anything.
"How did you have the key to the suitcase?" asks Mariam.

"Three years ago, Mr. Assi gave a copy of the key to our village chief, as a sign of trust. 'The money for your school will always be in this suitcase,' he said. 'You have the second key. You can check it any time.' A beautiful gesture. The chief kept the key in a box under his bed for three years."
"And Lassina?"
Joseph looks at the young man with great love.

"Lassina was my student. One of my best. He learned to read under the mango tree. His mother is from Assékro. He couldn't continue his studies — no money, no school after the primary level — so he works on the buses. When I learned that Assi would take this bus tonight, I asked Lassina to help me. I wanted to take back what belongs to the children. Only that. Not one franc more."
Lassina wipes his eyes. "I'm sorry, Vieux Père," he says to Vieux Konan. "I'm sorry, Inspector. But Teacher Joseph is right. He gave his whole life to our village."
"And the red earth on your shoes, Mr. Kouassi?" asks Mariam.

The old man looks at his shoes and laughs softly. "Assékro earth. I came to Abidjan this morning, directly from the village. I didn't have time to clean them. A real pastor would have clean shoes, I suppose."
"And the oil?"
"From the toilet floor. I went in to give the key to Lassina, while Fanta was singing."
Mariam closes her notebook. Everything fits. Every piece of the puzzle is in its place.
But now she has a much bigger problem. Because the law is the law. And the law says that Joseph Kouassi is a thief.
For a few seconds, nobody looks at Mr. Assi. Everybody is looking at the old teacher.
That is enough.

Mr. Assi jumps up, pushes Koffi out of the way, takes the big Bible from the seat, and runs to the back of the bus. Before anyone can move, he pulls the red handle of the emergency door. The door opens with a loud bang, and the cold night air comes into the bus.
Mr. Assi jumps out into the dark.
"HE'S RUNNING!" screams Ruth.
Mariam runs down the aisle. Black Diamond is already at the door — he is faster than everybody. Koffi follows him. They jump down onto the road.
Mariam jumps too. Outside, it is very dark. She can hear Mr. Assi running on the road, heavy and noisy, towards the forest. Black Diamond's long legs are catching up with him.
Then Mr. Assi turns off the road, into the tall grass, towards the trees. In ten seconds, he will be in the forest, and in the forest at night, nobody will find him.
And then something flies through the air.
It is a big basket of tomatoes.

It hits Mr. Assi on the back of the head. He falls forward into the grass with a loud "OOF!" Tomatoes roll everywhere. The Bible opens, and ten-thousand-franc notes fly up into the night like strange, beautiful birds.
At the emergency door of the bus, Tantie Akissi stands with her hands on her hips.
"Forty years at the market," she says proudly. "You think I can't throw a basket?"

Black Diamond and Koffi hold Mr. Assi on the ground. Mariam arrives. She doesn't have handcuffs — she is on holiday — so Tantie Akissi gives her a long yellow and blue pagne, and Mariam ties Mr. Assi's hands with it. Very tight.
"This is not legal!" Mr. Assi shouts. "I want my lawyer!"
"You'll have one," says Mariam. "In Bouaké."

It takes twenty minutes to find all the money in the grass with phone torches. Everybody helps: the market women, Fanta with Junior on her back, Ibrahim, Ruth and Koffi, even Vieux Konan. Nobody keeps a single note. When they count it on a seat in the bus, it is all there. Ten million francs.
Ruth looks at the money for a long time. Then she looks at Koffi. "Two million," she says softly. "Just two million, and all our problems..."
Koffi takes her hand. "No," he says. "That's the children's money. We'll find another way."
Ruth smiles at him through her tears. "I know. I just wanted to say it."
Vieux Konan starts the engine again. Twenty kilometres later, they arrive in a small village. On a little hill near the road, Mariam's phone finds one bar of network.
She makes two phone calls.

The first call is to the police in Bouaké. "This is Inspector Touré, from Abidjan. I am on the night bus from Adjamé, bus number 7. I have a man here, Bernard Assi, accused of stealing public money. Please wait for us at the bus station at five o'clock."

The second call is longer. She calls a friend from university, who now works for the Ministry of Education in Bouaké. She wakes her up. She tells her everything: the contract, the photos, the three wooden posts, the ten million francs from the village.
"Send me everything you have," says her friend, now completely awake. "This is very, very serious."
When Mariam comes back to the bus, Joseph Kouassi is waiting for her at the door. He holds out his two hands, wrists together.
"I am ready, Inspector."
Mariam looks at the old teacher's hands for a long moment. Hands that wrote on a blackboard nailed to a mango tree for thirty-one years.
"Mr. Kouassi," she says. "Stealing is stealing. Even from a thief. You know that. You are a teacher."
"I know."

"So you will come to the police station in Bouaké, and you will tell your story to a judge." She pauses. "But I will be there too. And I will tell the judge my story. About an old teacher who took back the money of six hundred people, and didn't keep one franc for himself."
The old man's eyes fill with tears.
"Put your hands down, Mr. Kouassi," says Mariam softly. "Sit down. It's a long way to Bouaké."
At ten to five, the night bus arrives in Bouaké.

The sky is starting to change colour: black, then dark blue, then a soft grey with a line of orange on the horizon. At the bus station, three police officers are waiting, with a car and a lot of questions.
Mr. Assi gets off first, his hands still tied with Tantie Akissi's pagne. The police officers look at the pagne, then at Mariam.
"We'll give you back your pagne, Tantie," says one of them.
"Keep it," says Tantie Akissi. "Wash it first."
Joseph Kouassi gets off next, with Lassina beside him. Mariam walks with them to the police car. Before he gets in, the old teacher turns around and looks at the bus, at all the faces in the windows.

The passengers start to clap. First the market women. Then Fanta, then Ruth and Koffi, then Ibrahim, then Black Diamond, who claps slowly, with his sunglasses on top of his head. Even Vieux Konan honks the horn three times.
Joseph Kouassi bows, like a teacher at the end of the school year, and gets into the car.

Mariam doesn't sleep that morning. She spends four hours at the police station, writing reports and answering questions. At ten o'clock, her friend from the Ministry of Education arrives with two inspectors and a lawyer. At eleven o'clock, they leave for Assékro, to see the three wooden posts with their own eyes.
At one o'clock in the afternoon, finally, Mariam knocks on the door of her mother's house.
Her mother opens the door. She has a bandage on her arm and a walking stick, but her eyes are bright.
"Mariam! My child! You came!"
"I came, Maman."
Her mother looks at her: at her tired face, her dusty clothes, the red marks of tomato on her shirt.
"What happened to you? Did you travel by bus or by war?"
Mariam laughs for the first time in fifteen hours. "Make me some tea, Maman. And sit down. It's a long story."
*Three months later.*
The new school in Assékro is not finished yet. But the walls are up, the roof is on, and the blue paint is drying in the sun.

The government gave the contract to a new company, and a team of inspectors comes every week to check the work. The village's ten million francs are in a bank account in the name of the school, and three people must sign to take out a single franc: the village chief, a woman from the market association, and the new headmaster.
The new headmaster is Joseph Kouassi.

The judge listened to his story for two hours. Then he gave him a suspended sentence: no prison, but no more mistakes. "You broke the law," the judge said. "But I think the law should be ashamed that it needed an old teacher to do its job."

Mr. Bernard Assi is in prison in Bouaké, waiting for his trial. The police found three other villages with "invisible" schools and two invisible health centres. Ibrahim Coulibaly wrote the full story. It was published in a big newspaper in Abidjan, with his name on it. He got a job offer the next week.
On the day the school opens, there is a big party in Assékro. Drums, dancing, food for everybody.

Tantie Akissi brings tomatoes — "for the party, not for throwing." Fanta comes with Junior, who can now walk, and his father in his soldier's uniform. Ruth and Koffi come too: they got married, and Koffi now repairs the new school's water pump for free. Black Diamond plays the guitar, and for the first time, the children of Assékro dance to live music in their own school yard.
Lassina is there in a clean white shirt. Next month, he starts evening classes in Bouaké. He wants to become a teacher.
Mariam Touré cuts the ribbon in front of the door. Then Joseph Kouassi gives her a small present wrapped in paper. She opens it.
It is the big black Bible with the square hole in the middle. The hole is empty now.
"For your office in Abidjan," says the old teacher. "To remember that sometimes, the best place to hide the truth is inside a book."
Mariam laughs and holds the Bible against her heart.
Then the children run into their new school, shouting and laughing, and the old mango tree stands alone in the field, finally free to rest.
**THE END**

title: The Night Bus to Bouaké
author: Léxi
desc: Un car de nuit entre Abidjan et Bouaké, onze passagers, dix millions de francs qui disparaissent… L'inspectrice Mariam Touré a jusqu'au lever du soleil. Roman complet.
